references.title: Troubleshoot connection quality in Azure Virtual Desktop

claims.says: Up to 150 ms shouldn't affect work without rendering or video, 150 to 200 ms is fine for text, over 200 ms might affect user experience.

references.title: Azure Virtual Desktop Insights glossary

claims.says: Input delay bands: good under 150 ms, acceptable 150 to 500 ms, poor 500 ms to 2 s, bad over 2 s.
Time to connect splits into user route, stack connected, logon (profiles, Group Policy, shell start, FSLogix) and shell start to shell ready; no target time is given.
Insights lists the recommended performance counters and their intervals for session hosts.

references.title: Use cases for Azure Virtual Desktop Insights

claims.says: Latency should generally be below 100 ms for ideal interaction; a session becomes broadly low quality over 200 ms.
Each session host's user input delay should ideally stay below 100 ms.
Use session history and idle host counts over time to design a scaling plan, then repeat to validate it.

references.title: Prerequisites for Azure Virtual Desktop

claims.says: Round-trip time from the client's network to the host pool's Azure region should be under 150 ms; put session hosts in the region closest to users.

references.title: Security recommendations for Azure Virtual Desktop
references.notes: The AVD product team's own security page. The Well-Architected AVD security page resolves to the same article and commit. The review checklist's G items (ref:review-checklists-avd) link into its sections.

claims.says: Microsoft secures the control plane and the physical layers; identity, user devices, apps, the session host OS, deployment configuration and network controls are the customer's.
Multi-session hosts suit standard users of one organization; users who need local admin get a personal host pool; users from different organizations get a separate tenant and subscription.
Turn on Defender for Cloud's enhanced security features and work from its Secure Score recommendations.
Require multifactor authentication for AVD sign-in and scope access with Conditional Access.
Collect audit logs (AVD diagnostics, the activity log, Entra sign-ins, session hosts) and monitor usage with Azure Monitor.
Set maximum inactive time and disconnection policies, and screen locks for idle sessions.
Separate admin access by tier, and don't give users local administrator rights on pooled hosts.
Run endpoint protection and an endpoint detection and response product on session hosts, with vulnerability assessment and regular patching.
Use Trusted launch (Secure Boot, vTPM, boot integrity monitoring) for session hosts; confidential VMs are the stronger option where needed.
Turn on Virtualization-based Security, HVCI and Credential Guard, and control which apps run with Windows Defender Application Control.
Restrict device redirection (drives, clipboard, printers, USB) to what each group of users needs.

references.title: Defender for Cloud compute security recommendations
references.notes: None of these is AVD-specific; they apply to session hosts as VMs. Reading Defender's own assessment results is cheaper and fresher than recomputing them.

claims.says: Defender for Cloud assesses VMs for an EDR solution, vulnerability findings, Secure Boot and vTPM on supported VMs, and the Guest Attestation extension, among others.

references.title: Intune security baselines for Windows devices

claims.says: Intune ships versioned security baselines (Windows, Defender for Endpoint, Edge and others) that enrolled devices, session hosts included, can be assigned and reported against.

references.title: Azure security baseline for Azure Virtual Desktop (Microsoft cloud security benchmark)
references.notes: Maps the benchmark's controls to what AVD supports, feature by feature, with whether each is on by default and who configures it. Claim IDs are the benchmark's own control IDs; we use them to place a security finding in a control family, as the WAF codes do for pillars. Only the controls the method uses are listed. It covers the AVD service itself; session hosts are VMs and also fall under the VM baseline. On 2026-10-20, LT-1's guidance text talks about Key Vault alerts, which looks like a copy error upstream.

claims.says: Private Link is supported for TCP RDP but not required or recommended without a specific need; RDP Shortpath covers private networks and the internet path is a fallback.
Use one central identity and authentication system (Microsoft Entra ID) for the service.
Restrict resource access based on conditions, through Conditional Access.
Follow least privilege with Azure RBAC, using the built-in AVD roles.
Encrypt sensitive data in transit.
AVD's own data at rest is encrypted with platform keys by default, with nothing to configure; customer-managed keys aren't supported for the service.
Turn on threat detection; the reference is onboarding session hosts to Defender for Endpoint.
Turn on resource logs for security investigation.
Build a secure configuration baseline into the session host image, or use a hardened image from a trusted supplier.
Run vulnerability assessments on session hosts.
Use endpoint detection and response on session hosts.
Use modern anti-malware on session hosts.

references.title: Troubleshoot issues using Performance Monitor (Windows Server)

claims.says: Processor time bands: up to 50% healthy, 50 to 80% worth watching, over 80% critical.
A processor queue of two or more per processor while CPU is high means looking for the processes using it.
Log counters over one or two working days, then look for patterns by day and hour rather than reacting to one reading.

references.title: Supported RDP properties
references.notes: The host pool's custom RDP properties are readable from the control plane, so device redirection can be judged without signing in to a host. Session host policy can still restrict further.

claims.says: Drive, clipboard, printer, USB, COM port, camera and WebAuthn redirection are each named host pool RDP properties with documented values.

references.title: Azure review checklists, Azure Virtual Desktop
references.notes: 130 items with short ID, category, WAF pillar, severity and Learn link. The AVD items have no Resource Graph query, so mapping evidence to them is ours (gap:checklist-mapping). Cite items by short ID, never by GUID.

claims.says: Don't offer both full desktops and RemoteApps from the same host pool to the same users (Security, high).
Configure the Azure Files share for Entra Kerberos authentication on Entra joined hosts (Security, medium).
Consider Start VM on Connect for personal host pools (Cost, low).
Send diagnostic settings for workspaces, host pools, application groups and host VMs to a Log Analytics workspace (Reliability, medium).
Decide whether to control or restrict internet outbound traffic from session hosts (Security, medium).
Evaluate a private endpoint for the Azure Files share (Security, medium).
Evaluate RDP Shortpath for clients on managed internal networks (Performance, medium).
Secure RDP sessions with policy (idle and disconnect limits, screen lock) (Security, medium).
Run anti-virus and anti-malware on session hosts (Security, high).
Assess disk encryption requirements for session hosts (Security, low).
Enable Trusted launch on Gen2 session hosts (Security, medium).
Trusted launch and a Gen2 image are requirements for Windows 11 (Security, high).
Consider screen capture protection for sensitive information (Security, low).
Restrict device redirection and drive mapping (Security, medium).
Users have no local administrator rights on session hosts (Security, high).
Enable Defender for Cloud for session host security posture (Security, medium).
Enable diagnostic and audit logging (Security, medium).
Assess whether custom RBAC roles are needed for AVD management (Security, low).
Restrict users from installing unauthorized applications (Security, medium).
Evaluate MFA and Conditional Access for AVD users (Security, medium).
Review and apply Zero Trust principles (Security, medium).
Keep the FSLogix profile storage in the same Azure region as the session hosts (Performance, high).
Configure the recommended antivirus exclusions for FSLogix (Security, medium).
Review and confirm the configured maximum FSLogix profile size (Cost, high).

references.title: Screen capture protection in Azure Virtual Desktop

Multi-session maximum users per vCPU: light 6, medium 4, heavy 2, power 1.
Keep multi-session VMs between 6 and 24 vCPUs; four cores is the lowest for a stable multi-session VM.

observations.observed: The landing zone's default RDP properties turn drive, USB and COM port redirection off but keep clipboard, printers, smart cards, WebAuthn and the camera, because users need them. Restricting redirection is a per-property trade-off, so the method reports each one kept on as a warn with its reason, not as a gap.
Latency measured from Cloud Shell says nothing about users, because Cloud Shell runs in an Azure datacenter. Measure round-trip time from the user's device, against endpoints verified to be regional.

The landing zone's minimum kit defaults to a 4-vCPU memory-optimized host, which is Microsoft's stated floor and below its 6 to 24 vCPU range, chosen for the smallest test cost. The reasoning that shared hosts run out of memory before CPU is our hypothesis; no measurement backs it yet.

Hardening the profile share to AES-256-GCM as the only SMB channel encryption denied every Entra Kerberos session; allowing AES-128-GCM as well, with CCM still off, let users in. Encryption in transit stays on, but the strictest setting isn't usable with Entra Kerberos, so the method treats AES-128-GCM plus AES-256-GCM as passing.
The landing zone deploys every session host with Trusted launch, Secure Boot and vTPM on, from Gen2 images, and the demo host pool ran on it with no boot or image problem.

Adopted as the landing zone's automatic sizing input, and its preflight warns above 6 sessions per vCPU. No real users have been measured against it, so the numbers are still Microsoft's prior, not our evidence.
The landing zone's image build keeps WDOT's Appx package removal off for this reason; no sysprep failure has been seen with it off. Not yet tested with it on.

WDOT's DiskCleanup category deletes every log, trace and event log file on the system drive, including an image build's own evidence before the image test reads it. The landing zone keeps that category off and cleans narrowly instead.
